content:
If you don’t live in a major city with streetcars, you might not think about streetcars. They were once the chief mode of public transit in North America. Most original urban streetcar systems were either dismantled in the mid-20th century or converted to light rail. Today, only Toronto still operates a streetcar network with an unchanged layout. Older surviving lines and systems remain in Boston, Cleveland, Mexico City, Newark, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, and San Francisco. These were often systems with tunnels, right-of-way lanes, and long-distance lines. Most have rebuilt their streetcar systems as light rail. About 22 North American cities, including Edmonton, Calgary, and San Diego, have installed light rail. Some run along historic streetcar paths. A few other cities and towns have restored a small number of lines to run heritage streetcars for public transit or tourists. Many are inspired by New Orleans' St. Charles Streetcar Line, the world's oldest continuously operating streetcar line.

Urban transit in North America began when horse-drawn omnibus lines started to operate from the 1820s to the 1880s. An example is Gilbert Vanderwerken's 1826 omnibus service in Newark, New Jersey. Soon, omnibus companies sought to boost profits from their wagons by increasing ridership. Horsecar lines simply ran wagons along rails set in a city street instead of on the unpaved street surface that the omnibus lines used. The wagon’s rolling resistance decreased when pulled on the rails. As a result, the average speed increased. A horse or team that rode along rails could carry more paying passengers per day than those that did not. North America's first streetcar line opened in 1832 from downtown New York City to Harlem by the New York and Harlem Railroad. This was followed by New Orleans in 1834 and Toronto in 1849 with the Williams Omnibus Bus Line.

Streetcars used horses or mules. Mules were thought to give more hours per day of useful transit service than horses. They were especially popular in southern cities like New Orleans. In many cities, streetcars drawn by a single animal were known as "bobtail streetcars," whether mule-drawn or horse-drawn. By the mid-1880s, 415 street railway companies in the U.S. operated over 6,000 miles of track and carried 188 million passengers per year using animal-drawn cars. Around the same time, Mexico had streetcars in around 1,000 towns, and many were animal-powered. In 1907, Mexico had 35 animal-powered streetcar lines in Veracruz state, 80 in Guanajuato, and 300  in Yucatán. However, during the nineteenth century, particularly from the 1860s to the 1890s, many streetcar operators switched from animals to other types of power. The advantages of eliminating animal power included not needing to feed or clean up waste.

The powers of electricity were on display at the World Cotton Centennial in New Orleans from December 1884 to June 1885. It featured displays with a lot of electric lights. There was an observation tower with electric elevators and many styles of electric streetcars. Montgomery, Alabama, established its electric streetcar system nicknamed the Lightning Route in 1886. The electrified streetcar system built in Scranton, Pennsylvania, in 1886 was the first to be run exclusively on electric power. That gave Scranton the nickname "The Electric City." By 1889, 110 electric railways had been started or planned on a few continents. By 1895, almost 900 electric street railways and nearly 11,000 miles of track had been built in the U.S. The rapid growth of streetcar systems led people to live outside the city and commute to work. Several communities that grew due to this new mobility were known as streetcar suburbs.
